title: What a p-value is not
objectives: Spot the common misreadings of a p-value.

screens.prose: A backtest of a new strategy gives $p = 0.03$ against $H_0$: no edge. Here are five readings of that number.

rows: If the strategy had no edge, a result at least this strong would turn up 3% of the time.
There is a 3% chance the strategy has no edge.
There is a 97% chance the strategy has a real edge.
The strategy's edge must be large.
Among many strategies with no edge, about 3% would look at least this good.

screens.question: Tap every statement that is true.

hints.text: A $p$-value is worked out assuming $H_0$ is true. Which statements assume that?
Two statements describe a world with no edge. The others claim something about the strategy itself.
Tap the first and the last. Each says how often a strategy with no edge would look this good.

feedback.correct: Both true statements assume no edge and ask how often data look this good.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only statements that assume $H_0$ and talk about the data.

byKey.all-but-size: You tapped the two readings that turn $p$ into a chance about the strategy. $p$ assumes no edge; it does not measure it.
byKey.r1: You read $p$ as the chance $H_0$ is true. $p$ assumes $H_0$ and asks how surprising the data are.
byKey.r2: You took $1 - p$ as the chance the edge is real. That needs to know how common real edges are.
byKey.r3: A small $p$ can come from a tiny edge measured on lots of data. $p$ mixes size with sample size.
byKey.r0: Tap the first statement too: it is the definition of $p$.
byKey.r4: The last statement is true as well. It is the definition, read across many strategies with no edge.

explain.text: $p$ is a chance computed in a world where $H_0$ holds: how often data would look at least this good. The first and last statements say exactly that. The others are claims about the strategy, which $p$ alone cannot make.

screens.prose: A research team tests 1,000 ideas a year. Each test has $\alpha = 0.05$ and power 0.8. The bars count the significant results by truth. Drag the share of ideas that are real.

derive.caption: {{round(b*100)}}% of ideas real: share of significant results that are real = {{fixed(0.8*b/(0.8*b+0.05*(1-b)), 2)}}

screens.question: As real ideas get rarer, what happens to the share of significant results that are real?

options.text: It falls, and quickly once real ideas are rare
It stays near 95%, because $\alpha = 0.05$
options.why: You read $1 - \alpha$ as the share of significant results that are real. Watch the caption as you drag left.

options.text: It stays at 80%, the power
options.why: Power is the share of real ideas that pass. The caption asks the reverse: the share of passes that are real.

options.text: It rises, because fewer ideas means fewer mistakes
options.why: Fewer real ideas leaves more noise to pass by luck. Drag to 1% and read the caption.

feedback.correct: Rare real ideas leave the noise bar to dominate.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag from 30% down to 1% and watch the caption.

explain.text: At 30% real, 240 of the 275 significant results are real. At 1%, only 8 of 57.5 are. The test is the same; only the base rate changed.

screens.prose: The $p$-value is $P(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0)$. What we usually want is the reverse, $P(H_0 \mid \text{significant})$. Now 10% of ideas are real, so the prior odds on a real edge are 1:9.
screens.question: What is $P(H_0 \mid \text{significant})$?

hints.text: Count the significant results in each bar.
There are $80 + 45 = 125$ significant results. Which of them have no edge?
$P(H_0 \mid \text{significant}) = 45/125$.

feedback.correct: 45 of the 125 significant results have no edge: 0.36.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the no-edge bar by both bars together.

byKey.alpha: You took $\alpha$ as $P(H_0 \mid \text{significant})$. That turns the conditional round: $\alpha$ is $P(\text{significant} \mid H_0)$.
byKey.real: 0.64 is the share that are real. The question asks for the share with no edge.
byKey.prior: 0.9 is the share of all ideas with no edge, before any test. Use only the significant ones.

explain.text: Of 125 significant results, 45 come from no edge, so $P(H_0 \mid \text{sig}) = 0.36$, not 0.05. In odds form, a pass multiplies the odds by $0.8/0.05 = 16$. Prior odds 1:9 become 16:9, so $P(\text{real} \mid \text{sig}) = 16/25 = 0.64$.

screens.prose: The team switches to data-mined signals, where only 1 in 100 is real. One passes the 5% test. A colleague says: “$p$ is below 0.05, so we are over 95% sure it is real.”
screens.question: What is $P(\text{real} \mid \text{significant})$ now?

hints.text: Per 1,000 signals, how many are real, and how many of those pass?
10 are real and 8 pass. Of the 990 with no edge, $0.05 \times 990 = 49.5$ pass.
$P(\text{real} \mid \text{sig}) = 8/(8 + 49.5)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the real passes by all the passes.

byKey.one-minus-p: You took $1 - p$ as the chance the signal is real. With 1 in 100 real, the noise passes swamp the real ones.
byKey.old: 0.64 was for a 10% base rate. Here only 1% of signals are real.
byKey.power: 0.8 is the chance a real signal passes. You want the chance a pass is real.

explain.text: Prior odds 1:99 times the ratio 16 give 16:99, so $P(\text{real} \mid \text{sig}) = 16/115 = 0.139$. The colleague's 95% confuses $1 - \alpha$ with a chance about the signal. Six passes in seven are noise.

screens.prose: Two backtests on the same idea. One gives $p = 0.049$ and the other $p = 0.051$. Their one-sided $z$ statistics are 1.655 and 1.635. The desk trades only below 0.05.
screens.question: What does the evidence say about the two backtests?

options.text: They are almost equally strong: the $z$ values differ by 0.02
The first shows an edge and the second does not
options.why: You let the 0.05 line split two results that are nearly equal. Evidence does not jump at 0.05.

options.text: The second should be dropped from the report
options.why: A $p$ of 0.051 is almost the same evidence as 0.049. Report both, with their effect sizes.

options.text: The first has a 95.1% chance of being real
options.why: That reads $1 - p$ as the chance the edge is real, which needs a base rate.

hints.text: Look at where the two lines sit on the $z$ axis.
The lines are 0.02 apart on a curve whose sd is 1.
Two $z$ values 0.02 apart are practically the same evidence. Only the 0.05 rule treats them differently.

feedback.correct: 0.049 and 0.051 are the same evidence, rounded to a rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two $z$ values, not the side of 0.05 they fall on.

explain.text: The two lines nearly coincide: $z = 1.655$ against 1.635. A threshold is a decision rule, not a law of nature. The evidence changes smoothly with $z$.

screens.prose: A factor earns 0.01% a day on average, with an sd of 1%. The study pools 100,000 stock-days.
screens.question: What is $z = \bar x/(s/\sqrt n)$?

hints.text: Write the mean and sd as decimals: 0.0001 and 0.01.
The standard error is $0.01/\sqrt{100{,}000} = 0.0000316$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the mean by $s/\sqrt n$.

byKey.no-n: You divided the mean by $s$ alone. The standard error is $s/\sqrt n$.
byKey.n-not-root: You divided $s$ by $n$. The standard error uses $\sqrt n$.
byKey.percent-mix: You mixed percent and decimals: write 0.01% as 0.0001 and 1% as 0.01.

explain.text: $z = 0.0001/(0.01/\sqrt{100{,}000}) = 3.16$, so $p \approx 0.0008$. Yet the edge is 1 basis point a day, less than most trading costs. With $n$ large enough, every true difference, however tiny, is significant.

screens.prose: A vendor's backtest of a signal reports $p = 0.05$. The sales deck says: “There is only a 5% chance this result is due to chance.”
screens.question: Which reading of $p = 0.05$ is correct?

options.text: If the signal had no edge, a result at least this strong would appear 5% of the time
There is a 5% chance the result is due to chance
options.why: That is $P(H_0 \mid \text{data})$, the conditional turned round. $p$ is $P(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0)$.

options.text: There is a 95% chance the signal works
options.why: That reads $1 - p$ as a chance about the signal. It needs the base rate and the power.

options.text: A repeat backtest would be significant 95% of the time
options.why: Repeat success depends on the power, not on $1 - p$.

hints.text: The shaded tail is computed under which hypothesis?
The whole curve assumes $H_0$. So $p$ is a chance about data, given $H_0$.
Pick the option that starts by assuming no edge and then talks about how strong results look.

feedback.correct: $p$ assumes no edge and measures how surprising the data are.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. $p$ is computed on the $H_0$ curve, so it assumes $H_0$.

byKey.due-to-chance: You read $p$ as the chance that chance explains the result, which is $P(H_0 \mid \text{data})$. With 10% of ideas real it was 0.36, not 0.05.

explain.text: The shaded tail is $P(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0)$. “The chance it is due to chance” is $P(H_0 \mid \text{data})$, the reverse. We found the reverse can be 0.36 or 0.86, depending on the base rate.

screens.prose: You turned $p$ round with base rates. For a significant result, Bayes in odds form gives $$\frac{P(\text{real} \mid \text{sig})}{P(H_0 \mid \text{sig})} = \frac{1 - \beta}{\alpha} \times \frac{P(\text{real})}{P(H_0)}.$$ With prior odds 1:9, power 0.8 and $\alpha = 0.05$: $$P(\text{real} \mid \text{sig}) = \frac{0.8 \cdot 0.1}{0.8 \cdot 0.1 + 0.05 \cdot 0.9} = 0.64.$$
screens.question: A test has power 0.5 and $\alpha = 0.05$; prior odds on a real effect are 1:4. What is $P(\text{real} \mid \text{sig})$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the prior odds by power over $\alpha$, then turn odds into a chance.

byKey.one-minus-alpha: 0.95 is $1 - \alpha$. It ignores both the prior and the power.
byKey.power: 0.5 is the power, $P(\text{sig} \mid \text{real})$. You want the reverse.
byKey.no-prior: You used odds 10:1, leaving out the prior odds 1:4.

explain.text: The likelihood ratio is $0.5/0.05 = 10$. Prior odds 1:4 become 10:4, so $P(\text{real} \mid \text{sig}) = 10/14 = 0.714$. Lower power means a weaker ratio, so a pass from a weak test is worth less.

screens.prose: An abstract reads: “We test momentum with 20 lookback windows. The best window earns 4% a year, with $p = 0.03$.” The paper reports nothing about the other 19.
screens.question: What is the main problem with that $p = 0.03$?

options.text: The window was chosen after looking, so $p$ no longer means what it says
0.03 is too close to 0.05 to count
options.why: That is the 0.049 against 0.051 worry. The bigger issue is that 20 windows were tried.

options.text: There is a 3% chance momentum is noise
options.why: That turns the conditional round again. And it ignores the 19 other tries.

options.text: 4% a year is too small to matter
options.why: 4% a year can matter. The question is whether it is real after 20 tries.

hints.text: If momentum had no edge at all, would the best of 20 windows still look good?
Each window has a 5% chance of $p < 0.05$ by luck. There were 20 chances.
Picking the best of 20 after looking makes a small $p$ likely even with no edge.

feedback.correct: Choosing after looking breaks the meaning of $p$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how the reported window was chosen.

explain.text: If the 20 windows were independent and all noise, $P(\text{at least one } p < 0.05) = 1 - 0.95^{20} = 0.64$. Choosing the test after seeing the data is called $p$-hacking. Level 3 shows how to correct for it.

screens.prose: A vendor says its signal is “99% significant”, meaning $p = 0.01$. Before paying, you ask for more.
screens.question: Which requests would actually help? Select all that apply.

options.text: The average edge per trade, with a confidence interval
How many signals they tried before this one
Results on data the signal was not built on
A smaller $p$ from a longer backtest of the same idea
options.why: A smaller $p$ can come from a tiny edge on more data. It says nothing about size or the number of tries.

options.text: Written confirmation of a 99% chance the signal works
options.why: No $p$-value gives that. It would need the base rate of working signals.

hints.text: $p$ hides two things: how big the edge is, and how many ideas were tried.
An interval shows the size; the number of tries shows how much luck was involved.
Ask for the effect with a confidence interval, the number of things tried, and out-of-sample results.

feedback.correct: Size with its uncertainty, the number of tries, and fresh data.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the requests that reveal the edge's size or how much searching was done.

explain.text: A confidence interval says how big the edge might be, which $p$ cannot. The number of tries says how much luck could explain it. Data the vendor never saw tests both at once.

ideas: A $p$-value is $P(\text{data at least this extreme} \mid H_0)$. It is not $P(H_0 \mid \text{data})$, and $1 - p$ is not the chance the effect is real.
Turning it round needs the base rate and the power: posterior odds = (power / $\alpha$) × prior odds.
$p$ says nothing about size, does not jump at 0.05, and loses its meaning when the test is chosen after looking.

formula.name: Odds after a significant result
formula.note: Ask for the effect size with a confidence interval, and the number of things tried.

summary.trap: “A 5% chance the result is due to chance” turns the conditional round. $p$ assumes $H_0$; it does not measure it.

quiz.prose: A backtest with power 0.3 for the edge we care about gives $p = 0.4$.
quiz.question: Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: The test is inconclusive: it would miss that edge 70% of the time
The signal has no edge
options.why: You read non-significance as no effect. With power 0.3, a miss is the usual outcome even for a real edge.

options.text: There is a 60% chance the signal has no edge
options.why: You turned $1 - p$ into a chance about the signal. $p$ cannot give that.

options.text: There is a 40% chance the signal is real
options.why: $p$ is not a chance that the signal is real.

feedback.correct: Low power makes a miss uninformative.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how often a real edge would also give a non-significant result.

explain.text: With power 0.3, a real edge gives a non-significant result 70% of the time. So $p = 0.4$ cannot tell a real edge from none. A bigger sample is the fix.

quiz.prose: In a field where 20% of tested ideas are real, a test with power 0.8 and $\alpha = 0.05$ gives a significant result.
quiz.question: What is $P(\text{real} \mid \text{significant})$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply prior odds 1:4 by $0.8/0.05$.

byKey.one-minus-alpha: 0.95 is $1 - \alpha$, which ignores the base rate.
byKey.prior: 0.2 is the share real before the test. A pass raises it.

explain.text: $\dfrac{0.8 \times 0.2}{0.8 \times 0.2 + 0.05 \times 0.8} = \dfrac{0.16}{0.20} = 0.8$. It matches the power here only by coincidence.

quiz.prose: Study A: an effect of 0.3 sd on 100 observations. Study B: an effect of 0.003 sd on 1,000,000 observations. Both give $z = 3$ and $p = 0.001$.
quiz.question: Which study found the larger effect?

options.text: A, by a factor of 100
They are the same: both have $p = 0.001$
options.why: You read $p$ as a measure of size. $p$ mixes size with sample size.

options.text: B, because it used more data
options.why: More data makes B's estimate more precise, not its effect larger.

options.text: We cannot tell without the $p$-values
options.why: The effect sizes are given: 0.3 sd and 0.003 sd.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the effects, not the $p$-values.

explain.text: $z = \text{effect} \times \sqrt n$: $0.3 \times 10 = 3$ and $0.003 \times 1{,}000 = 3$. Equal $p$-values can hide effects 100 times apart.

options.text: With zero true alpha, data this extreme would arise 2% of the time
There is a 2% chance the alpha is due to chance
options.why: That is $P(H_0 \mid \text{data})$, the conditional turned round.

options.text: There is a 98% chance the alpha is real
options.why: $1 - p$ is not the chance the effect is real.

options.text: The alpha is large
options.why: A small $p$ can come from a small alpha measured over a long time.

feedback.correct: $p$ assumes zero alpha and measures surprise.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. $p$ is a chance computed assuming $H_0$.

explain.text: $p = P(\text{data at least this extreme} \mid H_0)$. Every other reading needs a base rate or an effect size that $p$ does not hold.
